done.why: I had walked every open way I could find. East of the Round Room ended on a ledge over a river, the dam was boarded 'closed for inspection', two low passages ran under still black water, the maze was all alike and would not run backwards, and the hole beneath the altar politely turned me around. With the bar in the case and nothing left that would let me through, I checked my score (124 of 350) and left.

about: The old white house and the caves under it, the Zork I half remember, but rewritten line by line in a dry, wry voice that notices things: a mailbox less weathered than the house, a table nobody tidied, a railing that is 'the most reassuring thing you have seen in some time'. It is a smaller place than the original, and the edges of it are drawn with sentences instead of walls: a river with no boat, a dam closed by The Management, water that lies perfectly still, a hole that has waited this long and can wait a little longer. Running under it all is a thread about somebody careful who has been here ahead of me, clearing the crawlway, sorting fallen rock into neat heaps, coiling the rope because they expected to need it, barring the trap door. I never met them, and that is the question I came away carrying.

moments.note: The mailbox is 'a good deal less weathered' than the house. More than the original ever said about it, and a telling detail.
Boards nailed 'by someone in more of a hurry than a carpenter. Whatever the owners meant by it, they did not mean visitors.'
'Someone has been eating well, and has not been tidying up.' The table has a story.
The garlic is 'very much itself' and 'keeps certain company at a distance, and most other company too.'
The trophy case has 'the patient air of something that expects to be filled.'
The cellar crawlway has been cleared lately: rock stacked, fresh pick marks. Someone is working down here. New to me.
The troll: 'a great many teeth, not all of them his own', watching me 'the way a cook watches a chicken'.
The west hole is 'not so much an exit as a suggestion, and not a friendly one.'
Fallen rock sorted into heaps 'the way some people tidy a room they have no intention of using', and grit still trickling. The careful stranger again, and the fall is fresh.
Examining the heaps just repeats the cave-in text word for word. I wanted to get closer and could not.
Touching the rubble: the roof 'would rather finish on you than not.'
Every word I said came back at me: 'Bar bar ...', 'Listen listen ...'. Smiling, but briefly lost.
The platinum bar is 'quite silent, which in this room is a distinction.'
A draught comes out of the crack, 'and so, now and then, does an ant.'
East of the Damp Cave is a ledge over a river in a hurry and no boat. The map has been cut here, and said so in a sentence.
The Deep Canyon says I can hear flowing water, but 'listen' hears nothing out of the ordinary.
'FLOOD CONTROL DAM #3. CLOSED FOR INSPECTION. -- The Management.' A funny, in-world way of closing the road.
'The floor goes down under black water lying perfectly still, and does not come up again anywhere your light can reach.' A chill in it.
'You go back the way you came, with wet feet.'
The stairway down from the East-West Passage comes out at the Chasm, which I had already reached another way. Took a turn to see it was a loop.
The railing is 'the sort of thing a careful person makes something fast to before trusting the drop. It is the most reassuring thing you have seen in some time.' A hint delivered as a feeling.
The Dome Room names no exits at all, and 'exits' is not a word it knows. I had to guess at the compass.
'A dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.' Best image in the place.
'The signature in the corner is too modest to read.'
The chimney 'has room for you, a light to climb by and one thing more, and not an inch besides.' A rule written as a sentence.
The rope was 'coiled with more care than anything else in the attic was put away. Someone expected to need it.' The careful hand again, upstairs this time.
The axe 'does nothing a sword does not do better.' The writing politely told me to put it down.
The torch is carved with 'a procession of tiny figures, every one of them carrying a tiny torch.'
The bell is for calling 'the faithful, or the servants, or the dead; the temple does not say which.'
From the hole, 'a faint sound, like a great many people sighing a very long way off.'
The coffin's face is 'very sure of its place in the world'; Ramses 'has evidently been moved elsewhere since, which the face does not seem to know.'
Praying at the altar put me in a forest. Also a frustration: for so large a thing, no sentence at all, just 'Forest'.
'None has a branch low enough to climb, which saves a good deal of argument.'
A songbird 'with better taste in treasure than in architecture.'
The trap door stayed open this time. The house stopped barring me once I had come up the chimney.
The maze wall is 'solid, plain and entirely uninterested in you.'
East from where I had come west put me in a dead end; the maze does not run backwards and the walls give nothing to hold on to.
Out of the maze by luck into the Troll Room. Relief more than delight.
The hole would not take me: 'whatever is down there has waited this long and can wait a little longer.' The last edge, and the gentlest.

wished: To find whoever has been clearing the crawlway, sorting the rock, coiling the rope and barring the trap door. The place kept pointing at them (turns 40, 50, 132) and never let me meet them.
To go down the hole under the altar and hear what the sighing was (turns 162, 238).
To be told something when the prayer worked: the move from Altar to Forest (turn 183) had no sentence at all.
For the Dome Room to say which ways led out, or for 'exits' to be a word (turns 98-99).
Some way to tell one maze passage from another, even a scratch on a wall (turns 213-224).
To examine the heaps of sorted rock and get something closer than the room's own line again (turn 53).
To see the dam, even boarded; 'closed for inspection' made me want it more (turn 76).
For 'listen' to agree with the room about the water (turn 75).

lines.line: boarded across with planks nailed every which way, by someone in more of a hurry than a carpenter. Whatever the owners meant by it, they did not mean visitors.
lines.why: First sign that the place had been rewritten by someone with a voice, and that the house's history mattered.

lines.line: It has the patient air of something that expects to be filled.
lines.why: The whole game's premise in one line about a piece of furniture.

lines.line: Someone has cleared it lately: the fallen rock is stacked neatly along one side, and there are fresh pick marks in the roof.
lines.why: The first thread of the careful stranger, which became the thing I was reading for.

lines.line: He is watching you the way a cook watches a chicken.
lines.why: Funniest line, and it made the troll frightening at the same time.

lines.line: somebody has sorted the nearest of it into neat heaps, smallest nearest, the way some people tidy a room they have no intention of using.
lines.why: A character drawn entirely through the arrangement of rocks.

lines.line: the floor goes down under black water lying perfectly still, and does not come up again anywhere your light can reach. Whatever is beyond is under it.
lines.why: The best of the boundary lines: it closes the map and makes it sadder.

lines.line: It is the most reassuring thing you have seen in some time.
lines.why: A hint that reads like a feeling instead of an instruction.

lines.line: The chasm drops away from your feet into a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.
coiled with more care than anything else in the attic was put away. Someone expected to need it.
lines.why: The thread again, upstairs in the house: the stranger was here too.

lines.line: of the kind used to call the faithful, or the servants, or the dead; the temple does not say which.
lines.why: Three readings offered and none chosen, which is how the whole temple felt.

lines.line: a faint sound, like a great many people sighing a very long way off.
You decide that whatever is down there has waited this long and can wait a little longer.
lines.why: The way the world said it was over, without saying so.

fun.why: Nearly every object paid back a look, the troll fight and the echo room and the chimney rule were satisfying in small ways, and getting the coffin out by prayer felt earned. The maze (217-224) cost me some of it, and the silent teleport (183) was a flat note.

engagement.why: I kept examining because the examines kept giving, and the tidy stranger's traces made me want to follow them. I lost some pull when the edges all turned out closed and none of them led to that person.

difficulty.why: For a reader this was right: the puzzles announced themselves in prose (the railing wants a rope, the chimney takes one thing, the axe is worse than the sword), the echo answered to the obvious word, and prayer at an altar is a natural thing to try. Only the maze fought me, and it fought by being featureless rather than clever.

interestingness.why: The rewriting is interesting in itself, and the unresolved thread of someone careful working the caves ahead of me gave the place a question. The closed edges were drawn with wit. It loses a point because the thread goes nowhere I could reach.

prose.why: Dry, exact, and never showing off: 'not so much light as annoy', 'quite silent, which in this room is a distinction', 'the temple does not say which'. The voice is consistent from the mailbox to the hole, hints are delivered as observations, and boundaries are sentences instead of refusals. Small lapses only: the heaps reusing the cave-in text, a bare 'Forest' after the prayer, and the Dome Room naming no exits.
